The core step of a quantum attack on Bitcoin and Ethereum now fits in under 900 logical qubits within Google's gate budget. In three published attack designs, the machine would shrink by zero to about 28%.

On October 13, Jieyi Long of Theta Labs posted an 893-qubit circuit to ECDSA Fail, an open benchmark for the point addition that Shor's algorithm repeats to recover a private key. A day later he posted an 874-qubit version. Both stay below the 1,175 qubits and 2.7 million Toffoli gates Google proved for its own circuit in March.

Narrower circuits exist, down to 676 qubits, but all of them exceed Google's gate count. The 676-qubit one needs about 150 times as many.

Pierre-Luc Dallaire-Demers, a co-author of the ECDSA Fail paper, put the physical saving at 25% for the IonQ, Oratomic and Google attack designs. I checked each one.

- Google: about a quarter, if every part of the machine shrank with the qubit count.

- Oratomic: nothing with its published codes, and at most 16% with a code sized for 893 qubits.

- IonQ: about 28% fewer ions, but longer attempts, because the circuit needs about 1.6 times IonQ's Toffoli gates per addition.

Nobody has compiled a full attack around either circuit yet.

Anybody remember what happened to $AMD in 2022 after its huge run from 2019 through 2021?

It was still printing record quarters and raised guidance early in the year. It ultimately reported 44% revenue growth, helped by the Xilinx acquisition, and 25% growth in adjusted EPS.

The stock still lost roughly 66% over about 10 months. Rates went up, valuations came down, and PC demand weakened as the year went on.

Then it happened again from March 2024 through April 2025. Revenue grew 14% in 2024, data center revenue grew 94%, adjusted EPS grew 25%, and $AMD raised its data center GPU revenue outlook four times that year.

The stock still lost roughly 66% over 13 months. The decline continued even after the Fed started cutting rates.

Two massive drawdowns in four years. Annual revenue and adjusted earnings growth didn’t prevent either one.

And after both of those drawdowns, $AMD went on to have monster legs higher and make new highs. Recognizing the risk of a correction and recognizing the opportunity that develops afterward are both part of the job.

A company can keep growing while the market decides it’s willing to pay a whole lot less for that growth. Record results don’t make a stock immune to changing expectations, business headwinds or a reset in valuation.

That’s the part people struggle with when a stock starts “selling off for no reason.”

I’m not telling you a company is worthless or that it can’t be worth more down the road.

I’m simply providing technical analysis and pairing that with what I’m seeing in the options flow to say, “Yeah, maybe we’re gonna need to correct to the downside for a bit until we see clear signs of renewed buying demand.”

And when that demand returns and the chart and flow start improving, we reassess.

You can believe in a company’s future, respect the downside while crowded areas of the market reset, and still be ready to recognize the next opportunity when conditions improve.
